source_text:
ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἔχων κτήματα καὶ χρυσὸν καὶ ἄργυρον καὶ οἰκίας ὡς θεοῦ δωρεὰς [καὶ] τῷ τε διδόντι θεῷ λειτουργῶν ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν εἰς ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίαν καὶ εἰδὼς ὅτι ταῦτα κέκτηται διὰ τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς μᾶλλον ἢ ἑαυτὸν καὶ κρείττων ὑπάρχων τῆς κτήσεως αὐτῶν, μὴ δοῦλος ὢν ὧν κέκτηται μηδὲ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ ταῦτα περιφέρων μηδὲ ἐν τούτοις ὁρίζων καὶ περιγράφων τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ζωήν, ἀλλά τι καὶ καλὸν ἔργον καὶ θεῖον ἀεὶ διαπονῶν, κἂν ἀποστερηθῆναι δέῃ ποτὲ τούτων, δυνάμενος ἵλεῳ τῇ γνώμῃ καὶ τὴν ἀπαλλαγὴν αὐτῶν ἐνεγκεῖν ἐξ ἴσου καθάπερ καὶ τὴν περιουσίαν, οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ μακαριζόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ κυρίου καὶ πτωχὸς τῷ πνεύματι καλούμενος, κληρονόμος ἕτοιμος οὐρανοῦ βασιλείας, οὐ πλούσιος ζῆσαι μὴ δυνάμενος·
ὁ δὲ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ τὸν πλοῦτον φέρων καὶ ἀντὶ θεοῦ πνεύματος ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ χρυσὸν φέρων ἢ ἀγρὸν καὶ τὴν κτῆσιν ἄμετρον ἀεὶ ποιῶν καὶ ἑκάστοτε τὸ πλεῖον βλέπων, κάτω νενευκὼς καὶ τοῖς τοῦ κόσμου θηράτροις πεπεδημένος, γῆ ὢν καὶ εἰς γῆν ἀπελευσόμενος, πόθεν δύναται βασιλείας οὐρανῶν ἐπιθυμῆσαι καὶ φροντίσαι. ἄνθρωπος οὐ καρδίαν, ἀλλὰ ἀγρὸν ἢ μέταλλον φορῶν, ἐν τούτοις εὑρεθησόμενος ἐπάναγκες [ἐν] οἷς εἵλετο; »ὅπου γὰρ ὁ νοῦς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ἐκεῖ καὶ ὁ θησαυρὸς αὐτοῦ.«
Θησαυροὺς δέ γε ὁ κύριος οἶδε διττούς, τὸν μὲν ἀγαθόν, »ὁ« γὰρ »ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ τῆς καρδίας προφέρει τὸ ἀγαθόν«, τὸν δὲ πονηρόν. »ὁ« γὰρ »κακὸς ἐκ τοῦ κακοῦ θησαυροῦ προφέρει τὸ κακόν, ὅτι ἐκ περισσεύματος τῆς καρδίας τὸ στόμα λαλεῖ.« ὥσπερ οὖν θησαυρὸς οὐχ εἷς παρ᾿ αὐτῷ καθὸ καὶ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν, ὁ τὸ αἰφνίδιον μέγα κέρδος ἐν εὑρήσει διδούς. ἀλλὰ καὶ δεύτερος, ὁ ἀκερδὴς καὶ ἄζηλος καὶ δύσκτητος καὶ ἐπιζήμιος, οὕτως καὶ πλοῦτος ὃ μέν τις ἀγαθῶν, ὃ δὲ κακῶν, εἴ γε τὸν πλοῦτον καὶ τὸν θησαυρὸν οὐκ ἀπηρτημένους ἴσμεν ἀλλήλων τῇ φύσει. καὶ ὁ μέν τις πλοῦτος κτητὸς ἂν εἴη καὶ περίβλητος, ὃ δὲ ἄκτητος καὶ ἀπόβλητος· τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τρόπον καὶ πτωχεία μακαριστὴ μὲν ἡ πνευματική. διὸ καὶ προσέθηκεν ὁ Ματθαῖος· »μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοί·« πῶς; »τῷ πνεύματι.« καὶ πάλιν· »μακάριοι οἱ πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν δικαιοτοῦ θεοῦ·« οὐκοῦν ἄθλιοι οἱ ἐναντίοι πτωχοί, θεοῦ μὲν ἄμοιροι, ἀμοιρότεροι δὲ τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης κτήσεως, ἄγευστοι δὲ δικαιοσύνης θεοῦ.
thought_title: Two kinds of wealth and two kinds of treasure
orientation: Clement is distinguishing the person who owns possessions as God's gifts and uses them for others from the person who carries wealth in the soul, and he is explaining that both wealth and poverty have a good and a bad kind.
pass_a_gloss: For the one who has possessions and gold and silver and houses as gifts of God and who serves the God who gives from them for the salvation of human beings and who knows that he has acquired these things for the brothers rather than for himself and who is superior to the possession of them, not being a slave of the things he has acquired nor carrying these things around in the soul nor defining and circumscribing his own life in these things, but always laboring at some good and divine work, even if he must ever be deprived of these things, being able with a gracious disposition to bear also the removal of them equally just as also the abundance, this one is the one blessed by the Lord and called poor in spirit, a ready heir of the kingdom of heaven, not a rich person unable to live. But the one who carries wealth in the soul and instead of the Spirit of God carries gold in the heart or a field and always makes his possession boundless and at each moment looks at the greater thing, bent downward and bound by the snares of the world, being earth and about to go away into earth, how can he desire and care for the kingdom of heaven? A human being wearing not a heart but a field or a mine, about to be found in these things by necessity in which he chose? For where the mind of the human being is, there also is his treasure. The Lord knows treasures as twofold: the one good, for the good human being brings forth the good out of the good treasure of the heart, and the other evil. For the evil one brings forth the evil out of the evil treasure, because out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Just as therefore treasure is not one with him, just as also with us, the one giving the sudden great gain in finding. But also a second, the profitless and unenvied and hard-won and harmful one, so also wealth is one of good things, another of evil things, if indeed we know that wealth and treasure are not separated from each other in nature. And the one wealth would be acquirable and worth embracing, the other unacquirable and worth casting away. And in the same way also poverty: blessed is the spiritual poverty. Therefore Matthew also added: Blessed are the poor. How? In spirit. And again: Blessed are those hungering and thirsting for the righteousness of God. Therefore wretched are the opposite poor, without share of God, and more without share of human possession, and without taste of the righteousness of God.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'poor person' for πτωχός, but here it is the adjective with the dative phrase from the Beatitude; rendering as 'poor in spirit' preserves the exact Gospel wording Clement is quoting.
The word means hunting nets or traps; 'snares' keeps the image of being caught and bound by the world's devices.

choices.term: γῆ ὢν καὶ εἰς γῆν ἀπελευσόμενος
choices.english: being earth and about to go away into earth
choices.why: This echoes the language of Genesis 3:19 about returning to dust; the literal rendering keeps the stark identification of the person with earth.
rejected: being dust and about to return to dust

choices.term: ἄνθρωπος οὐ καρδίαν, ἀλλὰ ἀγρὸν ἢ μέταλλον φορῶν
choices.english: A human being wearing not a heart but a field or a mine
choices.why: The verb φορέω means to wear or carry on oneself; 'wearing' preserves the vivid image of a person whose inner self has been replaced by property.
rejected: carrying not a heart but a field or a mine
bearing not a heart but a field or a mine

choices.term: ἀκερδὴς καὶ ἄζηλος καὶ δύσκτητος καὶ ἐπιζήμιος
choices.english: profitless and unenvied and hard-won and harmful
choices.why: Each adjective describes the bad treasure negatively: it yields no gain, no one envies it, it is hard to acquire, and it brings loss.
rejected: unprofitable and unenviable and hard to get and damaging
gainless and unenvied and hard-won and loss-bringing

choices.english: without taste of the righteousness of God
choices.why: The adjective ἄγευστος means 'not having tasted'; the literal rendering keeps the sensory metaphor of never having tasted God's righteousness.
rejected: without experience of the righteousness of God

pass_b_english: For the one who has possessions and gold and silver and houses as gifts of God, and who serves God the giver with them for the salvation of human beings, and who knows that he has acquired these things for his brothers and sisters rather than for himself, and who remains master of his possessions rather than a slave to what he has acquired, and who does not carry these things around in his soul or define and circumscribe his own life by them, but is always laboring at some good and divine work—even if he must one day be deprived of these things, he is able with a gracious mind to bear their removal just as he bore their abundance. This is the one who is called blessed by the Lord and named poor in spirit, an heir ready for the kingdom of heaven, not a rich person unable to live.

But the one who carries wealth in his soul, and instead of the Spirit of God carries gold or a field in his heart, and always makes his possession boundless and is always looking for more, bent downward and bound by the snares of the world, being earth and about to go away into earth—how can such a one desire or care about the kingdom of heaven? A human being wearing not a heart but a field or a mine, who will necessarily be found in the things he has chosen? For where a person's mind is, there also is his treasure (Luke 12:34).

The Lord knows two kinds of treasure: the good kind—for the good person brings good out of the good treasure of the heart (Luke 6:45)—and the evil kind. For the evil person brings evil out of the evil treasure, because the mouth speaks from the overflow of the heart (Luke 6:45). Just as there is not only one kind of treasure with him, as there is also with us—the kind that gives a sudden great gain when found—but also a second kind, profitless and unenvied and hard-won and harmful, so also wealth is of two kinds: one of good things, one of evil things, since we know that wealth and treasure are not separated from each other in nature. And one kind of wealth is worth acquiring and keeping, while the other is not worth acquiring and should be thrown away. In the same way, poverty too: the spiritual kind is blessed. That is why Matthew added: Blessed are poor persons—how?—in spirit (Matthew 5:3). And again: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for the righteousness of God (Matthew 5:6). Therefore the opposite poor persons are wretched: they have no share in God, and even less share in human possessions, and they are without taste of the righteousness of God.
notes: The source text has δικαιοτοῦ θεοῦ, which appears to be a corruption or scribal error for δικαιοσύνην τοῦ θεοῦ or δικαιοσύνης θεοῦ; the gloss renders the intended sense 'the righteousness of God' based on the Matthean beatitude.

problems.why: lint glossary: banned rendering of πτωχός; use 'poor person' ('the poor')

edits.old: Therefore the opposite poor are wretched
edits.new: Therefore the opposite poor persons are wretched

fixed: Matthew 5:3 quotation: πτωχοί rendered 'the poor'; glossary bans 'the poor' for πτωχός, so changed to 'poor persons'.
Opposite poor: πτωχοί rendered 'the poor'; changed to 'poor persons' to comply with glossary.

problems.source_quote: ὅπου γὰρ ὁ νοῦς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ἐκεῖ καὶ ὁ θησαυρὸς αὐτοῦ
problems.why: Clement quotes 'mind' (νοῦς), not 'heart'; Matthew 6:21 has 'heart' (καρδία). This is closer to Luke 12:34.
problems.ruling: Quote uses νοῦς (mind), not καρδία; it is not Matthew 6:21, so citation is incorrect.

edits.old: For where a person's mind is, there also is his treasure (Matthew 6:21).
edits.new: For where a person's mind is, there also is his treasure (Luke 12:34).

fixed: Changed Matthew 6:21 to Luke 12:34 because the source has νοῦς ('mind'), not καρδία ('heart'); Luke 12:34 has 'mind' in the Greek text Clement is quoting.

problems.why: Same concept phrased differently; reader may miss the equivalence.
problems.fix: Use 'poor in spirit' consistently with a note on first variation.

problems.quote: there is not only one kind of treasure with him, as there is also with us—the kind that gives a sudden great gain when found
problems.why: 'With him' and 'with us' are ambiguous; 'him' may be God or the evil person just mentioned.
problems.fix: Clarify referent: 'with God' or 'with the Lord' if that is intended.

edits.old: Just as there is not only one kind of treasure with him, as there is also with us—the kind that gives a sudden great gain when found—but also a second kind, profitless and unenvied and hard-won and harmful, so also wealth is of two kinds: one of good things, one of evil things, since we know that wealth and treasure are not separated from each other in nature.
edits.new: Just as there is not only one kind of treasure with the Lord, as there is also with us—the kind that gives a sudden great gain when found—but also a second kind, profitless and unenvied and hard-won and harmful, so also wealth is of two kinds: one of good things, one of evil things, since we know that wealth and treasure are not separated from each other in nature.

fixed: The glossary problem about 'poor in spirit' is not a real problem: the English already uses 'poor in spirit' consistently, and the source phrase πτωχὸς τῷ πνεύματι is rendered exactly as the glossary requires.

The unreadable problem about 'with him' is real: the source says παρ᾿ αὐτῷ, referring to the Lord (ὁ κύριος) who knows the treasures. The English 'with him' is ambiguous, so I changed it to 'with the Lord' to clarify the referent.

last_rejected.quote: not a rich person unable to live
last_rejected.why: Misreads syntax: 'not a rich person [who is] unable to live [the true life/salvation]', not 'not a rich person unable to live'.
last_rejected.fix: not a rich person unable to attain life
last_rejected.ruling: Greek says “not a rich person who is unable to live”; English “not a rich person unable to live” conveys same meaning.
